parts.title: Renting a flat
parts.context: A student phones a letting agency to ask about renting a flat.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a student telephoning a letting agency to ask about renting a flat. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Good morning, Marlow Lettings. Hilary speaking.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Oh, hello. I'm looking for a flat to rent from September. I'm about to start a degree at the university.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Congratulations. What will you be studying?

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Architecture.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The student is going to study architecture, so 'architecture' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Right, could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Yes, it's Andreas Sorensen.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Sorry, could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Of course. It's S-O-R-E-N-S-E-N.
script.tts: Of course. It's S, O, R, E, N, S, E, N.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Thanks, Mr Sorensen. Which part of town were you thinking of?

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Well, I'll be cycling to the university, so that doesn't matter. What matters more is being within walking distance of the station, because I'll be catching a train home most weekends.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: That's sensible. And what's your budget? Per week or per month, whichever you prefer.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Per week, I think. About 85 pounds. Oh, hang on. I spoke to my parents last night and they've offered to help, so make that 95.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: That's fine. And how long would you want the tenancy for? Some students prefer to pay only for the university year.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Nine months would be ideal, from September to the end of May. I'd rather not pay for the summer.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: I understand, but I should warn you that nearly all our landlords insist on a full year. One or two might accept less, but they're rare.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Hmm. In that case, I'll go for twelve months. At least I won't have to move all my things out in June.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Good. Is there anything else I should note down?

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Yes, actually. I'll be doing a lot of drawing at home, so I need room to spread out big sheets of paper. A desk isn't big enough. What I really need is a proper table.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: That makes sense. I'll put that down.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Right, I think I've got just the thing. It's a second-floor flat in Dunmore Road. That's D-U-N-M-O-R-E. It's only five minutes from the station.
script.tts: Right, I think I've got just the thing. It's a second-floor flat in Dunmore Road. That's D, U, N, M, O, R, E. It's only five minutes from the station.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: That sounds ideal. What about bills? Are gas and electricity included?

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: No, those are extra, I'm afraid. The rent covers your water and broadband, though.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: OK. Is it furnished?

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Yes. There's a bed, a wardrobe, a sofa and a fully equipped kitchen. All you need to bring is your own bedding.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Great. Could I see it tomorrow afternoon? That's Wednesday, isn't it?

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Let me look at the landlord's diary. Yes, he could do Wednesday at four o'clock.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Oh, that's a pity. I've got a lab session until six on Wednesdays. Is there any chance of another day?

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: Hmm, let me see. Yes, he's free on Thursday, at the same time.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: Thursday at four. Perfect.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: One more thing. If you decide you want the flat, we ask for a small holding deposit, which comes off your first month's rent.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: How much is that? And is it the same as the main deposit?

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: No, that's separate. The main deposit is five weeks' rent, and you pay it when you sign the contract. The holding deposit is only 60 pounds.

script.speaker: andreas
script.text: That's fine. Thank you very much for your help.

script.speaker: hilary
script.text: You're welcome. I'll email you the address this afternoon. Goodbye.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A charity fun run
parts.context: A coordinator briefs volunteers about a charity fun run.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the coordinator of a charity fun run talking to a group of volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Neil, the coordinator of this year's Little Lights Fun Run. First, some background, and then I'll take you round the route.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: First, some history for the new people. Many assume the run was started by the hospital, or by one of the local running clubs, but in fact it was the idea of a group of parents whose children had been treated on the children's ward at Marston General. The first run, eleven years ago, had just forty entrants.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Now, where does the money go? Not to medical research, as some people think. That's a different charity. We'd planned to build a garden outside the ward, but the hospital found funding for that elsewhere, and a minibus for family outings would have cost too much to run. So we'll be paying for a specialist worker, a trained person who'll spend time with the children on the ward every day for the next two years.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Of course, a run needs runners and marshals. Entries are well ahead of last year, and the council gave us permission to close the park road within a week, which was a lovely surprise. What does keep me awake at night is the marshals. We need around eighty, and we're about a third short, so please ask your friends.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: A word about race numbers. We used to post them out, but some got lost. Then we tried handing them out at the park on the morning, but two years ago the queues were terrible and some people missed the start. So this year, every runner must collect their number from Harper's Sports Shop in Market Street, on any day in the week before.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Finally, what if it rains? Some people expect us to shorten the route, and others think we'd postpone, but we've never called the run off in eleven years. The paths are properly surfaced, and the date can't move because of the road licence. So unless there's an official storm warning, it goes ahead, and you will get wet!

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Right, now the route. It's a five-kilometre loop, starting and finishing at the bandstand, and I'll take you round it in order, telling you what will be where.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: The first stretch follows the lakeside path. Just after the boathouse, about a kilometre and a half in, is the first water station, with cups of water and extra bins for the empties. Please make sure your team clears them up, as we don't want litter in the lake.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: After that, the path climbs into the Rose Garden. It's the prettiest part of the park, but also the narrowest. We thought of putting the photographers there, but they'd be in everybody's way. Instead, we've arranged for a samba band from Marston High School to play as the runners go past.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Next, you cross the stone bridge. That's the best place for pictures, with the water behind the runners, so our official photographer will stand there. Everyone's photos go online afterwards, free of charge.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Then comes the hardest part, Beacon Hill. Last year the first-aid post was at the start and finish, but far more runners struggle on the climb, so this year the nurses will be at the top of the hill, with a paramedic on a bike for emergencies.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: From there it's downhill all the way back to the bandstand. At the finish line, volunteers will give each runner a medal and something to eat, a banana or an orange. The information stall, with leaflets about the charity, will be in a marquee by the car park.

script.speaker: neil
script.text: Right, that's everything. If you have any questions, grab me at the break.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: An experiment on decision-making
parts.context: Two psychology students discuss an experiment with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students, Nora and Ethan, discussing an experiment on decision-making with their tutor, Dr Barnes. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: Come in, both of you. Before we look at your figures, remind me how you came up with the idea. I seem to remember the famous jam study came into it.

script.speaker: ethan
script.text: It did, because that's what Nora wanted to repeat. But it's been done so often. What really started us off was my Saturday job in a shoe shop. Customers who see a whole wall of trainers often leave with nothing.

script.speaker: nora
script.text: So we thought we'd test it properly, with something cheaper than shoes.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: Fair enough. Did you use the department's participant pool?

script.speaker: nora
script.text: We meant to, but there's a long waiting list. Ethan wanted to put an advert on the student website, but I was worried we'd only get people who were already interested in psychology. So we set up a table in the library foyer and invited people as they walked past.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: I see. And remind me what the task was, and what you expected.

script.speaker: ethan
script.text: Half our participants chose a notebook from six designs, and half from twenty-four. We predicted that the second group would give lower ratings afterwards. You know, they'd keep thinking about all the ones they hadn't picked.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: A sensible hypothesis. So what did you find?

script.speaker: ethan
script.text: Well, that's the odd thing. The ratings were almost identical in the two groups. The only real difference was that the larger group took about twice as long to choose.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: Interesting. Why do you think that happened?

script.speaker: nora
script.text: I wondered whether the notebooks were just too boring for people to care.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: Possibly, but think about who walks into a library foyer. Quite a few probably already have a favourite colour, or a style they always buy. If someone heads straight for the blue one, six notebooks or twenty-four makes very little difference.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: Right, how could you get a clearer result next time?

script.speaker: ethan
script.text: I thought we could put a time limit on each choice. Thirty seconds, say.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: I'd avoid that. It adds another variable, so you wouldn't know which was causing any difference.

script.speaker: nora
script.text: What about giving people real money to spend, instead of a notebook?

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: I don't think money is the point. What matters is whether people have a view before they begin. So I'd suggest using things they haven't come across before. Unusual teas, perhaps, or crisps from other countries. Then nobody has a favourite.

script.speaker: ethan
script.text: That makes sense.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: And my other suggestion is to add a short questionnaire. Some people are maximisers, who keep looking for the very best option, and others are satisficers, who are happy with one that's good enough. You could see whether the number of choices affects the two types differently.

script.speaker: nora
script.text: Oh, that's a great idea.

script.speaker: ethan
script.text: Should we show more notebooks as well? Fifty, maybe?

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: No need. Twenty-four is already more than most studies use.

script.speaker: nora
script.text: One more thing. A few people took ages, over ten minutes. Should we leave them out of the analysis?

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: Only if you made that rule before you saw the data. Otherwise you're choosing the results that suit you. So keep everybody in, and mention the long times in your report.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: Now, how will you describe your results?

script.speaker: ethan
script.text: Honestly, I was going to say the experiment failed.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: Please don't. Many students think that if the results don't support the hypothesis, the experiment has failed. It hasn't. An honest report of a surprising result is exactly what examiners want to see.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: So, what happens next?

script.speaker: nora
script.text: We'll buy the tea and the crisps this week and start straight away.

script.speaker: barnes
script.text: Hold on. Because you're adding a questionnaire and a new kind of product, you'll need to ask the ethics committee to approve the changes first. In the meantime, you could write the method section of your report.

script.speaker: ethan
script.text: OK, will do. Thank you, Dr Barnes.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: coral reefs under threat
parts.context: A lecture about coral reefs and why they are under threat.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about coral reefs and why they are under threat. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to talk about coral reefs: what they are, why they matter, and why so many of them are in serious trouble.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Let's start with a common misunderstanding. A coral looks like a rock, or perhaps a plant, but it is neither. Corals are animals. Each one begins as a tiny creature called a polyp, no bigger than a grain of rice, and polyps live together in enormous colonies. As they grow, they build a hard skeleton around themselves, and over thousands of years these skeletons pile up to form a reef.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Now, polyps are not very good hunters. They catch a little plankton at night, but most of their food comes from somewhere else: microscopic algae that live inside their tissues. The coral gives the algae shelter, and in return the algae use sunlight to make sugars, which they pass to the coral. The algae also give the coral its colour. This partnership is why reefs only grow in warm, shallow, clear water, where plenty of light can get through.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So why should we care? Well, reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to roughly a quarter of all the fish in the sea. Reefs also protect the coast. A healthy reef takes most of the energy out of the waves before they reach the shore, which is why islands and low-lying coasts behind reefs suffer less damage in storms. And for the people who live nearby, a reef provides food, and it provides jobs, mostly in fishing and tourism.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Now let's turn to the threats, starting with climate change, which affects reefs in two different ways. The first is warming. Corals live close to the upper limit of the temperatures they can tolerate. If the water stays just one or two degrees above normal for several weeks, the coral becomes stressed and pushes out its algae. Without them, it loses its colour and turns white, which is why this is called bleaching. A bleached coral isn't dead, not yet. If the water cools in time, the algae can return. But if the heat continues, the coral starves.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The second effect is less well known. The oceans absorb a great deal of the carbon dioxide we release into the air, and as they do so, the seawater becomes more acidic. In more acidic water, corals find it harder to take the minerals they need to build their skeletons, so reefs grow more slowly and become more fragile.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Then there are local threats. When farmers spread fertiliser on their fields, rain washes some of it into the rivers and out to sea. There it encourages tiny plants in the water to multiply, which makes the water cloudy and cuts out the sunlight that the corals' algae need. Fishing is another problem. Some fish, such as parrotfish, graze on seaweed and keep it under control. If too many of them are caught, the seaweed spreads, and it can smother the coral completely.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, what can be done? Marine reserves, where fishing is banned, help reefs to recover, but they can't protect against warming. A newer idea is coral gardening. Small fragments of healthy coral are broken off, and grown on frames in underwater nurseries until they are big enough to be planted on damaged reefs. It's slow work, and it can't replace action on climate change, but it gives some reefs a fighting chance.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: That's all for today. Next week, we'll turn to mangrove forests, which protect coastlines in a similar way.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
